analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal terrorism insurance backstop through 2007 and adds group life coverage.
analysis.headline: With 22 bipartisan cosponsors, the Senate bill to extend the federal terrorism insurance backstop through 2007 never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the September 11 attacks, private insurers largely stopped covering terrorism, so Congress created a federal program in 2002: insurers must sell terrorism coverage, and the federal government pays most losses above a threshold the industry must first absorb. That program was set to end after 2005. This bill would extend it through 2007, raise the amount insurers pay before federal help kicks in, and extend the program to group life insurance for the first time. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners, businesses, and lenders keep access to terrorism coverage that private insurers would otherwise drop, and group life policyholders gain new protection. Insurers and reinsurers gain most directly: they keep collecting premiums while the federal government pays the large majority of losses above the industry's retention amount, so the insurance industry's balance sheets are shielded from a catastrophic attack.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, property owners, and commercial lenders

how_it_helps.text: It extends the terrorism risk insurance program, created after the September 11 attacks, through the end of 2007, so insurers must keep offering terrorism coverage to policyholders.
It continues the mandatory-availability requirement — insurers must keep offering terrorism coverage through the program's termination date — so property and business owners do not lose coverage.
It raises the industry-wide retention amount, the losses insurers must absorb before the federal government pays, to $17.5 billion for 2006 and $20 billion for 2007.
It extends the federal program to providers of group life insurance, whose policyholders' families would otherwise have no comparable terrorism loss protection.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost if the bill passes: the government pays the large majority of insured terrorism losses above the retention amount whenever a qualifying attack occurs, up to the program's cap. Absent an attack, the program costs little; if a major one occurs, the bill puts the public on the hook for losses the private sector would otherwise price or refuse.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, after a major attack

drawbacks.text: The federal government pays the large majority of insured terrorism losses above the industry-wide retention amount — set at $17.5 billion for 2006 and $20 billion for 2007 — so taxpayers carry a contingent liability that only comes due if a catastrophic attack occurs.
Insurers keep the premiums for terrorism coverage while the public backstop absorbs most catastrophic losses, which weakens the industry's incentive to price or manage that risk itself.
The bill extends the program with no long-term plan, instead directing a working group that includes insurance industry representatives to report recommendations for legislation by June 30, 2006.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a defensible transitional step: after 9/11, private insurers could not realistically price terrorism risk, and without a federal backstop coverage would disappear for commercial property buyers. The costs are real but contingent — taxpayers bear a potentially enormous share of losses if a major attack occurs, while insurers collect premiums in the meantime, and the industry's retention share, though rising under this bill, stays far below the federal share. Its biggest weakness is structural: it entrenches the private-market arrangement and defers any long-term solution to a future report, so honest supporters had to acknowledge they were extending the status quo rather than fixing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2004, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the bill on July 22, 2004, joined by eleven other senators from both parties as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action on it.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
Twenty-two senators cosponsored the bill — 10 Republicans and 12 Democrats — yet the bill never advanced past referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the inaction itself: insurers, reinsurers, and commercial property owners were left without an extension through this vehicle, while taxpayers took on no new contingent liability from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply stalled

sides.party_line_note: Support split almost evenly across parties — 10 of the 22 cosponsors were Republicans and 12 were Democrats — and the record shows no opposing votes, only committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill locks in an arrangement where insurers must sell terrorism coverage and collect the premiums, but the federal government pays the large majority of losses above an industry-wide retention. Property buyers get coverage they could not otherwise find, so the industry's gain and the public's gain partly run together.

The federal program absorbs the catastrophic terrorism tail risk that reinsurers would otherwise have to price or refuse, letting them operate as if that risk did not exist. Their gain comes at the public's expense as the contingent backstop.

industries.industry: Commercial real estate owners and mortgage lenders
industries.note: Without terrorism coverage, financing and leases on commercial property stall; the extension keeps that coverage available. This interest runs alongside property buyers' and lenders' ordinary business needs.
The bill extends the federal program to group life insurance for the first time, giving these insurers a federal backstop and their policyholders a guarantee of continued coverage.
